analysis.one_liner: Requires police agencies to report misconduct settlement costs to a public Justice Department database.
analysis.headline: Introduced in January 2026 with zero cosponsors and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require federal law enforcement agencies, plus states and cities that receive federal justice grants, to report each year how many misconduct lawsuits they settle or lose, how much the payouts cost, and where the money came from — tax budgets, insurance, or bonds. The Justice Department would have to post everything in a public, searchable database and commission an independent study of what the data shows. Police departments would for the first time have to show taxpayers the full bill for officer misconduct.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and communities, who would finally see — in one public database — how much police misconduct costs and who actually pays for it, whether that is the local budget, insurance premiums, or bonds paid off over years. Researchers and civil rights groups could compare agencies, and the Justice Department would have to issue annual best-practices guidance developed with law enforcement and civil rights organizations. States and cities that comply are protected from the penalty, and non-compliant jurisdictions' forfeited grant money would go to those that did comply.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities affected by misconduct

how_it_helps.text: Requires every federal law enforcement agency to collect, and report annually to the Attorney General, the number of misconduct judgments and settlements, the total amounts paid, the type of allegation (such as use of force, wrongful death, or false testimony), any personnel consequences for the officer, and the source of the money used to pay.

Requires states and cities receiving Byrne JAG grant funds to collect and report the same data for their police agencies, publish it on their own websites, and disclose specifically how payouts were financed — general budgets, agency budgets, bonds, liability insurance, or central risk pools.

Directs the Attorney General to build a public, searchable database of all reported misconduct settlement data within one year, excluding officers' personally identifiable information, so anyone can see which agencies cost taxpayers the most.

Gives the requirement teeth: a state or city that fails to comply can lose up to 10% of its Byrne JAG or COPS grant money for the year, and the withheld funds are redirected to jurisdictions that did comply.

Commissions a Government Accountability Office study after two years of data identifying which agencies spend the most on misconduct judgments, what drives those payouts, and how agencies could reduce misconduct, plus annual Justice Department reports with best practices developed in consultation with both law enforcement associations and civil rights organizations.

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies and the state and local governments that run them bear the cost: they must gather, verify, and report detailed data on misconduct judgments and settlements each year, and a jurisdiction that does not comply risks losing up to 10% of its federal Byrne JAG or COPS grant funding. The Justice Department pays for building and maintaining the database and verifying reports against court records and newspapers. The bill creates no new penalties for misconduct itself and imposes no direct cost on taxpayers beyond administration.
analysis.who_pays_short: Law enforcement agencies and local governments

drawbacks.text: It is a measurement bill, not a remedy: it documents the cost of misconduct but changes nothing about how police operate, and the independent study of what the data means would not even begin until two full years of data were collected.

Compliance is weakly enforced — the maximum penalty is a 10% reduction in two federal grant programs, which small jurisdictions might absorb rather than build reporting systems, and the Attorney General can grant 60-day extensions for good-faith efforts.

The database excludes personally identifiable information about officers and defers to the Privacy Act, so the public would see aggregate costs and allegation types but could not track individual officers' records.
The reporting burden falls hardest on small local governments and agencies, which must track insurance premiums, bond terms, and risk-pool contributions in addition to case data.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost side is modest — administrative reporting work and a conditional grant penalty — while the benefit is a durable public record of who pays for police misconduct and how much. The honest caveat is that transparency alone does not reduce misconduct, the study and best-practices phase arrives years after enactment, and the 10% grant penalty gives small jurisdictions room to ignore the law. As a low-cost accountability measure it weighs favorably, but its real-world impact depends entirely on whether the published data actually changes agency behavior.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Kaine introduced the bill and it was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Senator Tim Kaine introduced the Cost of Police Misconduct Act of 2026 in the Senate on January 29, 2026.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since.
No senator from either party has signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill with a single sponsor.
Congress remains in session until January 3, 2027, so the bill is still technically alive, but with no committee action it cannot reach the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, law enforcement agencies and the jurisdictions that prefer not to disclose misconduct payout data are better off, because the status quo — no federal reporting requirement — continues while the bill sits untouched in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies that avoid disclosing misconduct costs, for now

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (federal, state, and local)
industries.note: Agencies would have to compile and turn over detailed data on misconduct judgments, settlements, and personnel actions, and make the true fiscal cost of officer misconduct visible to the public. Their institutional interest in keeping this data scattered or private runs against the transparency the bill gives taxpayers.

industries.industry: Police unions and professional law enforcement associations
industries.note: Aggregate misconduct data — allegation types, personnel consequences, and payouts — would be published, increasing scrutiny of members' conduct, though officers' names stay private. The bill also gives associations a formal seat in drafting the Justice Department's best-practices guidance.

Jurisdictions receiving Byrne JAG funds face new reporting duties, including disclosing insurance premiums, bond costs, and risk-pool contributions, and risk losing up to 10% of federal justice grants for non-compliance. Compliant jurisdictions gain, since forfeited funds are reallocated to them.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is unlikely to advance. With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no committee action since its January 2026 referral, it would need a Judiciary Committee hearing and markup — and realistically Republican support — to reach the Senate floor before the Congress ends on January 3, 2027. Most single-sponsor bills in this position die quietly in committee; the realistic paths are reintroduction with cosponsors in a future Congress or inclusion of its reporting provisions in a larger justice or appropriations bill.
